metadata.title: Feasibility and treatment outcomes of simultaneous definitive chemoradiotherapy for elderly patients with synchronous hypopharyngeal and esophageal squamous cell carcinoma

sections.text: ABSTRACT Hypopharyngeal and esophageal squamous cell carcinoma may occur synchronously; however, optimal treatment strategies, particularly for elderly patients, remain undefined. We evaluated the feasibility and outcomes of simultaneous definitive chemoradiotherapy in this population. This single-institution retrospective study included patients aged ≥65 years who received definitive chemoradiotherapy for synchronous hypopharyngeal and esophageal squamous cell carcinomas between January 2002 and December 2022. Definitive chemoradiotherapy completion rate, objective response, overall survival, progression-free survival and adverse events were assessed. Fifteen patients were included (median age, 71 years; range, 67–85); all patients had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 or 1. The clinical stages of the carcinomas ranged from early to locally advanced, with the hypopharynx being the advanced site in seven patients (47%), the esophagus in six (40%) and both sites equally in two (13%). The definitive chemoradiotherapy regimen comprised three-dimensional conformal radiotherapy with 70 Gy in 35 fractions for hypopharyngeal carcinomas and 60 Gy in 30 fractions for esophageal carcinomas, with concurrent systemic chemotherapy, the most common being cisplatin/fluorouracil (seven patients, 47%). All patients completed the planned radiotherapy; although six patients (40%) required temporary radiotherapy suspension. Thirteen patients (87%) completed the planned chemotherapy. All patients achieved complete or partial response. The 2-year overall survival and progression-free survival rates were both 56%. All patients experienced grade ≥ 2 adverse events, but they were tolerable. Simultaneous definitive chemoradiotherapy is feasible and demonstrates favorable outcomes for elderly patients with synchronous hypopharyngeal and esophageal squamous cell carcinomas.

Approximately 10–20% of patients with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma develop synchronous or metachronous esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) [ 1 , 2 ], with a particularly high incidence of synchronous hypopharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (HPSCC) and ESCC [ 3 ]. This frequent coexistence is attributed to ‘field cancerization’, whereby prolonged exposure to shared carcinogenic substances leads to cumulative genetic alterations and the formation of multiple, independent tumors [ 4 ]. Common risk factors for HPSCC and ESCC, including smoking, alcohol consumption, male sex and advanced age, are also associated with the development of synchronous double cancers [ 1 , 2 ]. Treatment strategies for synchronous HPSCC and ESCC are complex because of the lack of established clinical guidelines and sufficient evidence. When neither tumor is amenable to minimally invasive transoral or endoscopic resection, curative treatment requires surgery or definitive chemoradiotherapy (dCRT). Limited retrospective studies comparing treatment outcomes during surgery, dCRT/RT and palliative treatment have demonstrated that surgery and dCRT/RT were associated with better prognosis than palliative treatment, with no significant difference in survival outcomes between surgery and dCRT/RT [ 5 ]. However, simultaneous surgical management of HPSCC and ESCC is technically challenging and has been associated with increased postoperative complications and reduced quality of life [ 6 ]. In contrast, simultaneous dCRT is reportedly feasible, with treatment completion rates of 95–97% and tolerable adverse events [ 7 , 8 ]. Reported outcomes of simultaneous dCRT include 2-year overall survival (OS) of 17–44% and 2-year progression-free survival (PFS) of 15–34% [ 7 , 9 ]. Treatment strategies for elderly patients with synchronous HPSCC and ESCC are particularly complicated. Several studies have reported that elderly patients receiving surgery or dCRT for either HPSCC or ESCC experience higher risks of adverse events and hospitalization compared with younger patients [ 10–14 ]. Conversely, other studies have found comparable survival and toxicity profiles for dCRT in elderly and younger patients [ 15 , 16 ], making its feasibility in elderly patients with either HPSCC or ESCC controversial. In elderly patients with synchronous HPSCC and ESCC, increased adverse events and reduced treatment feasibility are concerns due to the larger irradiation fields compared with elderly patients with either HPSCC or ESCC. Previous retrospective studies of dCRT for synchronous HPSCC and ESCC reported a median patient age of 53–64 years [ 7–8 ]. To the best of our knowledge, no study has specifically assessed the feasibility and treatment outcomes of simultaneous dCRT in elderly patients with synchronous HPSCC and ESCC. This single-institution retrospective study primarily aimed to analyze the feasibility of simultaneous dCRT in elderly patients with synchronous HPSCC and ESCC, including radiotherapy completion and suspension. Furthermore, chemotherapy completion and treatment outcomes, such as best overall response, survival and adverse events, were evaluated as secondary endpoints.

sections.section: Human Rights Statement And Informed Consent
sections.text: All procedures followed were in accordance with the ethical standards of the responsible committee on human experimentation (institutional and national) and with the Helsinki Declaration of 1964 and later versions. Informed consent or a substitute for it was obtained from all patients for being included in the study. The protocol for this retrospective study was approved by the institutional review board (No. 2912, approved 25 November 2022). To ensure that participants had the opportunity to decline participation, the study protocol was publicly posted on a website using an opt-out system.

All 29 patients who received simultaneous radiotherapy to the hypopharynx and esophagus between January 2002 and December 2022 were identified from our institution’s radiotherapy database. Figure 1 illustrates the inclusion and exclusion flow diagram of this study. Of these 29 patients, 22 were ≥ 65 years old at the start of radiotherapy. Seven patients were excluded—six received non-definitive radiotherapy, and one received radiotherapy without chemotherapy—leaving 15 patients for inclusion in this retrospective study. Because the primary endpoint of this study was to assess the feasibility of simultaneous definitive CRT in elderly patients, the patient selection intentionally allowed inclusion of patients with heterogeneous clinical stages. Medical records and radiotherapy planning data were reviewed to obtain the following information: age, sex, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group Performance Status (ECOG PS), histology of hypopharyngeal and esophageal cancers, clinical stage, systemic chemotherapy, observation period, radiotherapy completion and suspension, chemotherapy completion, best overall response, recurrence and survival outcomes and adverse events. The clinical stage of hypopharyngeal cancer was determined by otolaryngologists, diagnostic radiologists and radiation oncologists using pharyngeal fiberscopy, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging and 18 F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography–CT ( 18 FDG-PET-CT), following the Union for International Cancer Control TNM classification of malignant tumors, eighth edition (UICC-TNM, eighth edition) [ 17 ]. Esophageal cancer staging was assessed by gastroenterologists, esophageal surgeons, medical oncologists, diagnostic radiologists and radiation oncologists based on findings from upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, CT and 18 FDG-PET-CT, also according to the UICC-TNM eighth edition [ 17 ]. Treatment strategies were determined by a multidisciplinary tumor board. According to the treatment strategies in our institution, if either hypopharyngeal or esophageal cancer was superficial and suitable for minimally invasive treatment, such as transoral or endoscopic resection, minimally invasive treatment was provided first, followed by surgery or dCRT for the other site. When both cancers exceeded the criteria for minimally invasive treatment, simultaneous dCRT was generally preferred, particularly for elderly patients, due to the high invasiveness of simultaneous surgery.

Radiotherapy for hypopharyngeal cancers was delivered using four mega-voltage (MV) photons to a total dose of 70 Gy in 35 fractions over 7 weeks, while esophageal cancers were treated with 10 MV photons to a total dose of 60 Gy in 30 fractions over 6 weeks. Treatments were administered using a linear accelerator (Clinac iX, Varian Medical Systems, Palo Alto, CA, USA). All radiotherapy was planned using three-dimensional conformal techniques. Intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) was not applied due to the specifications of the linear accelerator available for treating the included patients. Supplementary Table 1 presents the details of radiotherapy planning. Briefly, the initial irradiation fields included the primary tumors, metastatic lymph nodes and locoregional lymph nodes up to 40 Gy, followed by a boost of 20–30 Gy to the primary tumors and metastatic lymph nodes. The hypopharyngeal and esophageal regions were treated on the same day using separate irradiation fields due to different beam arrangements. The use of elective nodal irradiation to the locoregional lymph nodes area was determined individually based on tumor location, clinical stage and patient condition by radiation oncologist in charge. The junction between the hypopharyngeal and esophageal irradiation fields was positioned between the superior border of the sternum and the level of the cricoid cartilage, at a level where neither primary tumors nor metastatic lymph nodes were present. Approximately 5-mm junction margin was applied, and beam arrangements were carefully adjusted to ensure that the dose at the junction did not fall below 50% of the prescribed dose. No junction shift was performed during the treatment course. When grade 4 adverse events were observed, radiotherapy was suspended until the toxicity resolved to grade 3 or lower. For grade 3 adverse events, radiotherapy was suspended at the discretion of treating physicians. Prophylactic gastrostomy placement for treatment-related nutritional impairment was not routinely performed at our institution. When oral intake became insufficient due to treatment-related adverse events, nutritional support was provided at the discretion of the treating department, either via central venous nutrition or nasogastric tube feeding.

Chemotherapy regimens were determined by the treating physicians based on the more advanced tumor site, clinical stage, patient age, ECOG PS score and laboratory findings. Six regimens were used: cisplatin/fluorouracil (PF), docetaxel, nedaplatin/fluorouracil (FGP), cisplatin, docetaxel/cisplatin/fluorouracil (TPF) and tegafur/gimeracil/oteracil. Supplementary Table 2 shows the details of dosing, administration schedule and cycles of each regimen during radiotherapy. The first chemotherapy cycle was initiated almost simultaneously with radiotherapy. When grade ≥ 3 adverse events occurred, the subsequent chemotherapy cycle was delayed until the toxicity resolved to grade 2 or lower. Furthermore, if necessary, chemotherapy was administered at a reduced dose or discontinued depending on patient age, ECOG PS, laboratory data and the severity of adverse events in the previous cycle.

Follow-up examinations after dCRT included pharyngeal fiberscopy, upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and CT performed at intervals of approximately 3–6 months. If these findings were difficult to evaluate the treatment outcomes, 18 FDG-PET-CT was applied. The best overall response was assessed according to the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors version 1.1 [ 18 ]. In cases of recurrence, additional therapy was considered by the treating physicians. The interval of OS was defined as the duration from the initiation of radiotherapy to death from any cause. The interval of PFS was defined as the duration from the initiation of radiotherapy to the first day of identifying either progression or recurrence or to death without recurrence. The curves and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) of OS and PFS were analyzed using the Kaplan–Meier method. All analyses were performed using Bell Curve for Excel version 3.20 (Social Survey Research Information Co., Ltd., Tokyo, Japan). Any adverse events potentially related to CRT were recorded using the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0 [ 19 ]. Adverse events that occurred between the initiation of dCRT and 3 months after its completion were considered acute adverse events, while those occurring 4 months or later after completing dCRT were considered late adverse events.

A total of 15 patients were included in this study. Table 1 shows patient characteristics. The median age was 71 years (range, 67–85 years), and all patients were male. The clinical stages of HPSCC and ESCC ranged from early to locally advanced. All three patients with ESCC at clinical stage 4B were classified as such due to supraclavicular lymph node metastases that were included in the irradiation fields, and none of the patients with clinical stage 4B disease included in this study had organ metastasis or distant lymph node metastasis besides the supraclavicular lymph node. When comparing the clinical stages of HPSCC and ESCC in each patient, the worst sites of clinical stage were the hypopharynx in seven (47%), the esophagus in six (40%) and the same in two (13%). Three patients were considered operable for both HPSCC and ESC; however, the patients preferred organ-preserving treatment. In the remaining patients, either one or both primary tumors were deemed inoperable. The most frequently used systemic chemotherapy was PF in seven patients (47%). Detailed information regarding the operability, treating department, rationale for chemotherapy selection, chemotherapy regimen with actually delivered dose (%) and cycles, application of elective nodal irradiation, recurrence site and savage treatment in each patient is provided in Supplementary Table 3 . Table 2 presents the treatment outcomes. The median observation period was 14 months (range, 3–164 months) for the entire cohort, and 28 months (range, 7–164 months) among the six surviving patients. All patients completed the planned radiotherapy, and nine of the 15 patients (60%) did not require radiotherapy suspension. Six patients (40%) required radiotherapy suspension. Of these six patients, only four patients (24%) needed radiotherapy suspension related to dCRT adverse events, and the remaining two patients needed radiotherapy suspension due to a radiotherapy machine malfunction in one (6%), and a national holiday in the other (6%). The median duration of radiotherapy suspension among the six patients was 7 days (range, 5–32 days). The completion rate for planned chemotherapy was 13/15 (87%), and two patients who received TPF or FGP were excluded from further chemotherapy after receiving one course due to acute grade 4 hematological adverse events. Five patients required dose reduction and/or a reduction in the number of chemotherapy cycles during dCRT. Among nine patients receiving regimens including cisplatin, three patients (33%) achieved a cumulative cisplatin dose of ≥200 mg/m 2 . Adjuvant chemotherapy after dCRT was administered to two patients (13%), as detailed in Supplementary Table 3 . All patients achieved an objective response, with nine patients achieving a complete response and six patients a partial response. During the observation period, seven patients (47%) experienced recurrence. Distant organ metastases, including lung metastases in four patients (27%) and pleural dissemination in one patient (7%), were more common (five patients, 33%) than locoregional recurrence (two patients, 13%). Among patients who experienced recurrence, one patient underwent endoscopic submucosal dissection as salvage treatment. No patient underwent salvage surgery or salvage radiotherapy. Detailed post-recurrence management is summarized in Supplementary Table 3 . Nine patients (60%) died during the observation period; of these, seven deaths (47%) were cancer-related, and two (13%) were non-cancer-related. The two non-cancer-related deaths were due to infectious pneumonia 11 months after CRT and acute myocardial infarction 93 months after dCRT. Figure 2 shows the OS and PFS rates. The median overall OS was 31 months, with 1-year and 2-year OS rates of 64% (95% CI, 38–90%) and 56% (95% CI, 29–83%), respectively. The median PFS was 26 months, with 1-year and 2-year PFS rates of 56% (95% CI, 30–83%) and 56% (95% CI, 30–83%), respectively. Table 3 presents the adverse events related to dCRT. All patients experienced adverse events of grade ≥ 2 during the observation period. Acute adverse events were grade ≤ 3 in most patients, although two patients (13%) experienced grade 4 acute hematological adverse events. No patient experienced grade 4 late adverse events. No grade 5 adverse events were observed in any of the included patients. Nutritional support was required in the majority of patients due to acute non-hematological adverse events including pharyngitis, esophagitis and dysphagia. Six patients (40%) received central venous nutrition and six (40%) required nasogastric tube feeding because of inadequate oral intake, whereas three patients (20%) completed treatment with oral intake alone. All patients were weaned from central venous nutrition or nasogastric tube feeding within one month after completion of radiotherapy.

In this retrospective study of elderly patients with synchronous HPSCC and ESCC, simultaneous dCRT was feasible and demonstrated favorable local response, survival outcomes and tolerable adverse events. All patients completed the planned radiotherapy, and most completed the planned concurrent chemotherapy. Objective responses (complete or partial) were achieved in all patients, which likely contributed to the observed favorable survival outcomes. Although all patients experienced grade ≥ 2 adverse events, no treatment-related deaths occurred. All 15 elderly patients completed the planned radiotherapy; however, six patients (40%) required radiotherapy suspension (median, 7 days; range, 5–32 days). This completion rate is comparable to the 95–97% reported in previous studies of younger patients with median ages of 53–64 years, despite the higher median age in this study (71 years; range, 67–85 years) [ 7 , 8 ]. Most previous studies on concurrent dCRT for synchronous HPSCC and ESCC did not adequately describe treatment suspension or its causes. One retrospective study with a median patient age of 64 years reported treatment suspension 53% of patients for 1–4 weeks, which is comparable to our findings [ 8 ]. These results support the feasibility of simultaneous dCRT for synchronous HPSCC and ESCC in elderly patients. Regarding treatment efficacy in this study, all patients achieved objective responses with complete or partial responses, and the 2-year OS was 56%, with both the 1-year and 2-year PFS also being 56%. Although several clinical stages of HPSCC and ESCC were included in this study and previous retrospective studies, these outcomes compare favorably with previous reports showing an objective response rate of 94% [ 8 ] and 2-year OS and PFS of 17–44% and 15–34%, respectively [ 7 , 9 ]. Nevertheless, the inclusion of patients with heterogeneous disease stages introduces the possibility of stage-related selection bias, and thus the survival outcomes should be interpreted cautiously. The finding that the 1-year PFS was 56% indicates that nearly half of the patients experienced progression or recurrence within the first year, raising the possibility that simultaneous dCRT targeting the less advanced primary site might not have been necessary in some patients. Conversely, the finding that identical 1-year and 2-year PFS indicate that a subset of patients achieved durable disease control beyond 1 year, suggesting that simultaneous dCRT may provide sustained tumor control in selected patients. In this study, seven patients died from disease recurrence. Locoregional recurrence occurred in only two patients (13%), and the most recurrent sites were distant organ metastases in five patients (33%). These findings suggest that dCRT provides effective locoregional control for synchronous HPSCC and ESCC; however, improved survival outcomes may require more intensive adjuvant or salvage systemic therapies after dCRT, as well as more appropriate patient selection, particularly for those at lower risk of distant metastasis. All patients in this study experienced grade ≥ 2 adverse events. The incidence of acute hematological toxicity of grade 3–4 was 60%, higher than the 24% reported in a previous study with a median age of 64 years [ 8 ]. Similarly, acute mucositis or pharyngitis with grade 3 and any late grade ≥ 3 adverse events were higher in this study, at 53% and 27%, respectively, compared with 12% and 0% in the previous study [ 8 ]. Despite the higher frequency of severe adverse events in this elderly cohort (≥ 65 years) compared with younger patients in previous studies, all adverse events were tolerable. No treatment-related deaths were observed in this study; however, careful management is essential, as a previous study reported treatment-related deaths in three of 51 patients (6%) [ 7 ]. Elderly patients generally have reduced tolerance to both radiotherapy and chemotherapy; therefore, careful patient selection and vigilant management of adverse events are necessary when administering dCRT for elderly patients with synchronous HPSCC and ESCC, where irradiation fields are larger than for each site alone. The optimal dCRT strategy, whether simultaneous or sequential, for synchronous HPSCC and ESCC remains uncertain, and direct comparative evidence is limited. A retrospective study suggested that sequential dCRT was not inferior to simultaneous dCRT in terms of survival and may be associated with lower toxicity [ 7 ]. Nevertheless, adverse events in synchronous HPSCC and ESCC, regardless of whether treatment was delivered sequentially or simultaneously, tended to be more frequent than those reported for dCRT of either HPSCC or ESCC treated alone [ 20 , 21 ]. However, the potential impact of prolonged overall treatment duration must also be considered. Sequential dCRT may require more than 4–5 months to complete, and the potential burden associated with such prolonged treatment duration should also be considered, particularly in elderly patients. Extended treatment courses may contribute to cumulative physical deconditioning and an increased risk of secondary complications such as delirium. In this context, determining whether simultaneous or sequential dCRT is preferable cannot be standardized and should be individualized, considering overall condition, disease stages, social circumstances and patient preference. Simultaneous dCRT may be reasonable when the patient’s general condition is preserved and shortening overall treatment duration is desirable, whereas a sequential approach may be appropriate for patients with limited tolerance to extensive irradiation. The present study provides supportive data regarding the feasibility and anticipated toxicity of simultaneous dCRT in this clinical setting. This study has several limitations. First, this was a retrospective, single-institution study, resulting in heterogeneous treatment regimens, especially for chemotherapy, and treatment suspensions were determined at the discretion of the treating physicians. In addition, because the primary aim of this study was to evaluate feasibility of simultaneous dCRT, patients with heterogeneous clinical stages were intentionally included. Consequently, survival outcomes may have been influenced by selection bias related to stage distribution and should therefore be interpreted with caution. Therefore, the generalizability of these results is uncertain, and prospective, multi-institutional clinical trials are warranted. Second, elderly patients were uniformly defined as those aged ≥65 years. However, previous research has shown that performance status, nutritional status, body weight, comorbidities and medical histories are also clinically important for evaluating elderly patients with cancer. Comprehensive assessment tools, such as the Geriatric-8, may be more appropriate for patient selection in studies of elderly populations [ 16 , 22 ]. Due to the retrospective design, some information was unavailable, and the Geriatric-8 criteria could not be applied in this study. Third, a three-dimensional conformal radiotherapy method, which is now less commonly used for head and neck cancers, was employed in this study due to the radiotherapy machine specifications available at our institution during the study period. In current clinical practice, IMRT is preferred because it allows more precise dose delivery to tumor sites while minimizing radiation exposure to surrounding organs. At our institution, IMRT has been used for radiotherapy of both HPSCC and ESCC since the radiotherapy machine was upgraded in 2024. Although the radiotherapy techniques used in this study differ from current clinical practice, three-dimensional conformal radiotherapy is likely associated with higher complication rates than IMRT. Since this study demonstrated feasibility and favorable outcomes even with a three-dimensional conformal radiotherapy, improved outcomes can be expected with IMRT. In addition, recent studies in radiotherapy for head and neck cancer and ESCC have suggested that elective nodal irradiation may be safely omitted in selected patients [ 23 , 24 ]. Although elective nodal irradiation was generally performed in the present study, given the advanced and of the patients and the presence of synchronous malignancies, a more limited irradiation field confined to the primary tumors and lymph node metastases may be a reasonable strategy. Despite these limitations, this study suggests that simultaneous dCRT is an effective treatment strategy for elderly patients with synchronous HPSCC and ESCC, for whom an optimal treatment approach has not yet been established. In conclusion, this retrospective study indicated that simultaneous dCRT for elderly patients with synchronous HPSCC and ESCC is feasible, with a radiotherapy completion rate of 100% and acceptable treatment suspensions, a chemotherapy completion rate of 87%, favorable treatment responses and tolerable adverse events.
